title: Who’s who in the Zoo – Tom Donlon
content:
Meet Tom Donlon, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Minnesota, who studies the Milky Way’s structure, evolution, and what it can tell us about dark matter. Tom shares why our Galaxy is wrinkly, what makes citizen science communities so powerful, and how Zooniverse volunteers are helping build a first-of-its-kind catalogue of shell galaxies.

Name: Tom Donlon (Postdoctoral Researcher)

Location: University of Minnesota Twin Cities

Zooniverse projects: Galaxy Zoo: What the Shell?, Artifact InSPECtor, Clump Scout II

What is your research about?

My work mainly involves understanding the structure of the Milky Way, the galaxy where we live. I’m interested in how it grows, changes, and evolves, with the ultimate goal of learning whatever we can about the dark matter inside our Galaxy. This has led me to think about a pretty broad range of objects — old stars, pulsars, variable stars — and how we can use them in creative and interesting ways to learn about the makeup of the Milky Way. I’ve also spent time working on the chemical composition of our Galaxy, its dynamic structure like waves and wiggles, and shell galaxies.

How do Zooniverse volunteers contribute to your research?

title: Georeferencing with Zooniverse!
content:
Where exactly was a museum specimen collected? A new Zooniverse project invites volunteers to help turn location information from museum records into points on a map, making biodiversity data easier for researchers to use. The project also introduces new mapping tools that will eventually support many different kinds of research on Zooniverse.

Yesterday, we launched a brand-new project: Notes from Nature – Putting Biodiversity on the Map. This project invites volunteers to help georeference museum specimen records by matching locality descriptions to places on a map. Museum specimen labels include locality information to describe the place where a specimen was collected. Georeferencing is the process of converting that locality information into geographic coordinates (e.g. latitude and longitude).

Prior to this project, the Notes from Nature research team would ask volunteers to transcribe specimen records in Zooniverse, then export the locality data to GEOLocate for georeferencing. GEOLocate includes tools for automated georeferencing (based on the transcribed locality information), and the data would then be reviewed and corrected on the GEOLocate platform.
